draft.title: Business responsibilities to consumers
card: A business has duties to the people who buy from it. Australian law sets many of these duties, and the government can act when a business breaks them.
Safety
Products must meet safety standards, so they do not harm people when used as intended.
Honest information
Ads, labels and prices must be truthful. A business must not mislead buyers about what a product is or what it can do.
Recalls
If a product is found to be unsafe, the business must recall it. It asks buyers to stop using the product and return it for a fix, a replacement or a refund.
draft.remember: Businesses must sell safe products, tell the truth about them and recall any that turn out to be unsafe.

a.q: Which action shows a business meeting its responsibility to give honest information?
opts: A label that lists what is in the snack bar truthfully
A snack bar that is sold at a lower price than rivals
A snack bar that is made in a clean, modern factory
A snack bar that is sold in shops across the country
a.why: Honest information means the label tells buyers the truth about the product. Selling at a low price or in many shops says nothing about whether buyers are told the truth. A clean factory relates to safety, not to what buyers are told.
a.clue: Look for the option about what buyers are told.

b.q: Leo's company sells toy cars. It finds that the wheels on one batch can snap off and be swallowed by small children. What must the company do?
opts: Recall the batch and ask buyers to return the cars
Lower the price of the batch to sell it quickly
Wait for buyers to complain before taking any action
Add a note to the website and keep selling the cars
b.why: A product found to be unsafe must be recalled, so buyers stop using it and can return it. Lowering the price or only adding a note leaves unsafe cars with children. Waiting for complaints delays the recall when a risk is already known.
b.clue: The company already knows the product is unsafe.

a.best: A label that lists what is in the snack bar truthfully

b.best: Recall the batch and ask buyers to return the cars

a.q: Which action shows a business meeting its duty to give honest information?
opts: Listing all the ingredients on a snack bar's label
Testing a snack bar to make sure it meets safety standards
Recalling a snack bar after it is found to be unsafe
Calling a snack bar sugar free when it contains sugar
a.why: Honest information is about what buyers are told, and a full ingredient list tells them the truth about the product. Testing for safety and recalling unsafe products are real duties too, but they are the safety and recall duties. Calling a sugary bar sugar free misleads buyers.
a.clue: Which duty is about what buyers are told?

problems.detail: The card says that if a product is found to be unsafe, the business 'must' recall it. In Australia most recalls are voluntary. Suppliers must notify the ACCC within two days of a voluntary recall, and the government can order a compulsory recall. The flat 'must' overstates the law, though it follows the chapter's wording of this point. Consider wording such as 'is expected to recall it, and the government can order a recall'. The 'must' in question b, its why and the remember line rest on the same overstatement.

'Products must meet safety standards' suggests that every product has a safety standard to meet. Mandatory safety standards cover only some product types, such as toys for young children and bicycle helmets. A small softening such as 'Many products must meet safety standards' would be more accurate.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the whys match the card. The card overstates Australian law in two places: it says businesses must always recall unsafe products (most recalls are voluntary, though the government can order one), and it implies every product has a safety standard.
